provisions_triggered.name: Due Process / Law of the Land

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: In re Adoption/Guardianship of Rashawn H.
key_cases.holding: Reversing a termination of parental rights, the Court held that a juvenile court may terminate parental rights only if it finds, by clear and convincing evidence and with findings tied to the statutory factors, that the parent is unfit to continue the parental relationship or that exceptional circumstances make continuing it detrimental to the child's best interest.
key_cases.relevance: Rashawn H. is Maryland's controlling statement of the TPR substantive standard and burden of proof that governs every termination decision.
key_cases.quote: the kind of unfitness or exceptional circumstances necessary to rebut the substantive presumption must be established by clear and convincing evidence, not by the mere preponderance standard

key_cases.case_name: In re Adoption/Guardianship of Ta'Niya C.
key_cases.holding: Vacating a denial of termination, the Court clarified that Rashawn H. did not displace the best-interest standard: unfitness and exceptional circumstances are measured through, not apart from, the child's best interest, which remains the governing standard in TPR cases.
key_cases.relevance: Ta'Niya C. fixes the relationship between the parental presumption and the best-interest standard that decides every Maryland TPR case.
key_cases.quote: we reexamine the law in this area and confirm once again that the child's best interest is the prevailing standard in these determinations

key_cases.holding: The Court held that purely custodial (Ross) factors have no place in a TPR analysis under FL § 5-323, but that the juvenile court's incidental reference to them did not taint findings otherwise properly made under the statute, so termination was affirmed.
key_cases.relevance: H.W. confines the TPR inquiry to the statutory factors and forbids comparing the parent to the foster placement as if it were a custody contest.
key_cases.quote: Although factors pertaining exclusively to custody have no place in TPR assessments under FL § 5-323, the juvenile court did not abuse its discretion

key_cases.holding: The Court held that a juvenile court abuses its discretion when it declines to terminate parental rights and instead leaves the child indefinitely in third-party custody after finding that neither parent can ever safely care for the child.
key_cases.relevance: It is the Supreme Court of Maryland's clearest statement that internally inconsistent findings cannot justify withholding termination.
key_cases.quote: The finding that Father was not unfit is contradicted by the juvenile court's finding that reunification with either Father or Mother was not attainable within the foreseeable future

key_cases.case_name: In re Adoption of Jayden G.
key_cases.holding: The Court affirmed termination, holding that whether to stay a TPR case while an appeal of a permanency-plan change is pending is committed to the juvenile court's discretion and that the court properly considered the child's attachment to his foster parents.
key_cases.relevance: It governs the sequencing of permanency-plan appeals and TPR proceedings, a recurring trap for parents' counsel.
key_cases.quote: whether to stay a TPR case is within the juvenile court's discretion

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that due process requires at least clear and convincing evidence before a State may terminate parental rights, and left to the States the choice of any standard equal to or higher than that.
key_cases.relevance: Santosky is the federal constitutional floor that Maryland's clear-and-convincing TPR standard implements.
key_cases.quote: We hold that such a standard adequately conveys to the factfinder the level of subjective certainty about his factual conclusions necessary to satisfy due process.

extended_foster_care_age: Up to the 21st birthday, and only while the young person meets one of five conditions: completing secondary education or a program leading to an equivalent credential; enrolled in an institution providing post-secondary or vocational education; participating in a program or activity designed to promote or remove barriers to employment; employed at least 80 hours per month; or incapable of any of those due to a medical condition documented in the case plan (COMAR 07.02.11.04B). Not eligible for out-of-home placement if married, in the military, or not complying with those conditions (COMAR 07.02.11.04C). Re-entry: the juvenile court has jurisdiction over a former CINA whose commitment to the local department was rescinded after age 18 but before age 20 years 6 months and who did not exit foster care due to reunification, adoption, guardianship, marriage, or uniformed services duty, and that jurisdiction continues until age 21 (Md. Code, Cts. & Jud. Proc. § 3-804(b)(2) and (c)).

common_failures: Failure to prove unfitness by clear and convincing evidence
Santosky v. Kramer standard not met
